title: Concept of Health Care Financing
path: Health Care Financing and Insurance Scheme

headings.title: Introduction to Health Care Financing
headings.content: Health care financing is a critical component of health systems strengthening, particularly within the context of nursing practice and health economics in Nigeria. It refers to the function of a health system concerned with the mobilization, accumulation, and allocation of money to cover the health needs of the population, individually and collectively. The primary objective of health care financing is to ensure that all individuals have access to effective public health and personal health care services without suffering financial hardship. For nursing students, understanding this concept is vital because the availability of financial resources directly dictates the quality of patient care, availability of essential medications, staffing levels, and infrastructure in health facilities. In developing nations like Nigeria, health care financing has historically relied heavily on out-of-pocket payments at the point of service. This approach often leads to catastrophic health expenditures, plunging vulnerable families into poverty and creating significant barriers to timely medical and nursing care. As future nursing professionals, students must comprehend how financial systems operate to advocate effectively for health policies that promote equity, reduce financial barriers, and improve health outcomes across urban and rural communities. A robust financing system ensures sustainable resources for disease prevention, health promotion, and curative services, forming the bedrock of a functional health care delivery system.

headings.title: Core Functions of Health Care Financing
headings.content: Health care financing is built upon three core functions: revenue collection, pooling, and purchasing. Revenue collection is the process by which a health system raises money from various sources, such as taxes, health insurance contributions, out-of-pocket payments, and donor assistance. Effective revenue collection must be progressive, meaning that contributions are based on the ability to pay rather than the risk of illness. The second function, risk pooling, involves accumulating prepaid revenues on behalf of a population to share the financial risk of falling ill. Pooling ensures that healthy individuals subsidize the sick, and wealthy individuals subsidize the poor, preventing any single person from bearing the full cost of a major illness. The final core function is purchasing, which involves transferring pooled funds to health care providers to deliver specific interventions. Strategic purchasing is essential here, meaning that payers actively select the most cost-effective and high-quality services, medicines, and technologies rather than passively reimbursing bills. For nursing students, understanding these functions helps explain how hospitals are funded, why certain services are prioritized, and how efficient allocation impacts the availability of nursing supplies and equipment at the bedside.

headings.title: Sources of Health Care Funds
headings.content: The generation of financial resources for health care comes from multiple channels, each with distinct implications for equity and sustainability. The primary sources of health care funds include government allocations through general taxation, social health insurance contributions, private voluntary health insurance, out-of-pocket spending by households, and external aid or donor funding from international organizations. General taxation relies on income, value-added, and corporate taxes collected by the government, which are then budgeted to the health sector. While tax-based systems can be equitable, they often suffer from low budgetary allocation in developing nations due to competing national priorities like education and infrastructure. Social health insurance (SHI) involves mandatory contributions from formal sector employees and employers, often subsidized by the government to cover informal workers and the vulnerable. Private health insurance caters mostly to high-income earners who can afford private premiums. Out-of-pocket spending remains a major source of financing in Nigeria, posing severe equity challenges. Additionally, external donor funding from partners like WHO, USAID, and global health initiatives provides vital support for specific disease programs, such as HIV/AIDS, malaria, and immunizations. Nurses must understand these funding sources to appreciate the financial constraints under which health facilities operate and to advocate for increased domestic resource mobilization.

headings.title: Mechanisms of Risk Pooling and Purchasing
headings.content: Mechanisms of risk pooling and purchasing are pivotal for achieving financial protection and health system efficiency. Risk pooling can be fragmented or integrated. In fragmented systems, numerous small insurance pools exist, which weakens their purchasing power and limits cross-subsidization between healthy and sick members, or rich and poor. Integrated or national pooling systems, conversely, cover larger populations, spreading financial risks more effectively and giving purchasing agencies stronger leverage to negotiate prices with healthcare providers. Purchasing mechanisms dictate how health providers are paid. Traditional purchasing methods include fee-for-service, where providers are paid for every service or test rendered, which often encourages over-servicing and escalating costs. Modern strategic purchasing utilizes alternative payment models such as capitation (a fixed payment per patient enrolled per month) and diagnosis-related groups (DRGs), which incentivize efficiency, quality care, and cost containment. For nurses, understanding these mechanisms is important because purchasing models influence hospital operations, staffing ratios, and the availability of clinical resources. Strategic purchasing encourages providers to focus on preventive care and patient outcomes rather than just the volume of procedures performed, aligning financial incentives with professional nursing values.

headings.title: Overview of Health Insurance Systems in Nigeria
headings.content: The landscape of health insurance systems in Nigeria reflects a mix of public and private initiatives designed to alleviate the burden of out-of-pocket spending. At the national level, the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA) Act establishes the legal framework for mandatory health insurance across the country. The NHIA aims to secure financial access to quality health care for all Nigerians. Nigeria operates various health insurance schemes, including the Formal Sector Social Health Insurance Programme, which covers federal government workers and organized private sector employees; the Informal Sector Programme, designed for artisans, traders, and community members; and vulnerable group funds aimed at providing free care for pregnant women, children under five, the elderly, and the indigent. Additionally, many states have established State Health Insurance Agencies (SHIAs) to implement mandatory health insurance at the sub-national level, bringing coverage closer to grassroots populations. Despite these structures, population coverage remains relatively low, particularly in the informal sector, due to issues of trust, awareness, and affordability. As patient advocates, nursing students and practicing nurses play a crucial role in educating patients about NHIA enrollment, guiding them through facility registration, and ensuring that insured patients receive appropriate, uncompromised care.

headings.title: Challenges of Health Care Financing in Developing Countries
headings.content: Developing countries, including Nigeria, face persistent challenges in health care financing that undermine health system performance and population health. A primary obstacle is low domestic resource allocation, as many governments fail to meet international targets such as the Abuja Declaration, which recommended allocating at least 15% of the national annual budget to health. This underfunding results in dilapidated health infrastructure, acute shortages of essential medicines, and poor remuneration for healthcare workers, including nurses. Another significant challenge is the dominance of out-of-pocket expenditures, which account for a large percentage of total health spending, driving vulnerable populations into extreme poverty when health crises occur. Furthermore, the large size of the informal economy makes revenue collection and risk pooling extremely difficult, as informal workers lack regular payroll deductions. Administrative inefficiencies, corruption, and poor financial management further drain available resources. External donor dependency also poses a sustainability risk when donor priorities shift or funding cycles end. For nursing students, understanding these systemic barriers is essential for contextualizing the daily operational challenges faced in clinical practice, such as working with limited consumables, and highlights the need for systemic health sector reforms.

headings.title: Strategies for Achieving Universal Health Coverage
headings.content: Achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) requires deliberate, multi-faceted financing strategies designed to ensure that all people receive the quality health services they need without financial hardship. A foundational strategy is increasing domestic resource mobilization through innovative taxation, such as taxes on sugar-sweetened beverages, tobacco, and alcohol, which both generate health revenue and discourage unhealthy behaviors. Expanding mandatory prepayment mechanisms, such as social and community-based health insurance, is also crucial to transition populations away from catastrophic out-of-pocket payments. Governments must prioritize budgetary allocations for primary health care (PHC), as strengthening PHC is the most cost-effective way to achieve UHC and deliver essential preventive and curative services to rural and underserved populations. Additionally, improving purchasing efficiency by shifting from passive fee-for-service models to strategic purchasing ensures that funds are tied to quality and health outcomes. Equity-focused subsidization policies must be enforced to guarantee that vulnerable groups—such as pregnant women, children under five, and the elderly—receive free or subsidized care. As future health advocates and nurse leaders, students must understand these strategies to actively participate in health policy discussions, support community health insurance initiatives, and advocate for equitable resource distribution.

headings.title: The Role of Nurses in Health Care Financing and Resource Allocation
headings.content: Nurses play a critical, multifaceted role in health care financing and resource allocation, extending far beyond direct bedside patient care. Because nurses represent the largest workforce in healthcare and are present at every level of service delivery, they possess frontline insights into resource utilization, waste, and unmet patient needs. In resource allocation at the unit or hospital level, nurse managers make vital decisions regarding staffing mix, inventory control, and the efficient use of medical consumables to prevent wastage. Furthermore, nurses are key patient advocates; they help patients navigate complex health insurance schemes, assist with NHIA registration, and connect vulnerable patients to social welfare or financial aid programs. In policy arenas, nurse leaders contribute to health economics discussions, advocating for increased health sector funding, fair remuneration, and the inclusion of nursing services in insurance reimbursement packages. Educating patients on cost-effective wellness practices and preventive care also reduces the economic burden of chronic disease management. For nursing students, developing financial literacy and resource management skills is essential to becoming effective leaders who can optimize patient outcomes while operating within the economic realities of modern health systems.
